item.title: Bayesian Comparison of Covid Origins Hypotheses
item.description: arXiv:2610.29766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applying standard Bayesian methods to the most reliably known unclassified facts about the Covid epidemic allows crude estimation of the odds for research-related vs. purely zoonotic origins. Here a broadly inclusive zoonotic hypothesis is compared with a rather specific subset of the research-related hypothesis defined by known prior work and grant proposals. The important observations are the type of virus, the city of the first outbreak, the lack of known prior hosts, the anomalous early pattern of evolution, and two specific features of the viral sequence. The resulting odds strongly favor research. The odds remain fairly strong under inclusion of uncertainties in prior odds.
item.dc:creator: Michael B. Weissman

item.title: When to retire: the cultural evolution of post-reproductive oblique teaching
item.description: arXiv:2610.30135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teaching is ubiquitous across human societies. Instruction from parents to offspring is the most fundamental form of teaching, explained primarily through kin selection and inclusive fitness. Instruction to non-kin, known as oblique teaching, also plays a dominant role in modern societies, where teaching is often institutionalized. Nonetheless, it remains puzzling how or when oblique teaching can evolve. Here we address the evolution of oblique teaching by developing a mathematical model of stage-structured populations. Younger individuals engage in a useful activity, called hunting, and reproduce. At some point in life, they cease contributing directly to hunting and reproduction, and instead serve exclusively as teachers who increase the hunting expertise of the young. We refer to this transition in life stage as retirement, and we analyze the evolution of the retirement rate, and the resulting frequency of post-reproductive teachers, in a population subject to a global carrying capacity. We find that retirement and teaching can evolve without kinship or inclusive fitness, but only in populations above a threshold size. Unlike in classical adaptive dynamics, the evolutionarily stable retirement rates depend on the absolute population size of a mutant type upon introduction. In many regimes, evolution produces fewer teachers than would maximize the population's per-capita hunting returns or intrinsic birth rate. A mutant that differs only slightly from the resident type generally cannot invade from a minority, so teaching cannot emerge through gradual evolution. The mechanism we describe is therefore available to cultural evolution, where a distinct norm for retirement and elder care may be adopted by a sub-population simultaneously. Our account is thus tied closely to theories of cultural evolution, including the "information grandmother hypothesis" of Henrich and Henrich.
item.dc:creator: Hirotaka Goto, Joshua B. Plotkin

item.title: Learning Epidemic Threshold Equations from Simulation: REEBLRA, an Interpretable Bayesian Classification Framework for Reproduction Numbers
item.description: arXiv:2610.29399v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The basic reproduction number, $R_0$, is central to infectious-disease modelling, yet analytic expressions can be difficult to derive for high-dimensional, nonlinear, or structurally complex models. We introduce REEBLRA ($R_0$ Equation Estimation using Bayesian Logistic Regression Algorithm), an interpretable framework that learns explicit surrogate equations for epidemic thresholds from parameter--response data. Rather than directly regressing $R_0$, REEBLRA estimates $\Pr\{R_0(\boldsymbol\theta)>c\}$ for parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ and threshold $c$. It provides a binary equation for classifying epidemic invasion ($R_0>1$) and successive threshold equations defining ordered brackets that approximate $R_0$, the expected number of secondary infections caused by a typical case in a fully susceptible population. The resulting equations support parameter screening, sensitivity interpretation, threshold classification, and exploratory analysis when analytic derivation is cumbersome. Bayesian logistic regression using standardized polynomial-like features and proper weakly informative priors yields regularized estimates, posterior uncertainty, and finite coefficients under complete or quasi-complete separation. We establish a mechanistic--surrogate concordance principle linking the full fitted-score gradient to the local gradient of $\log R_0$ under explicit regularity and tangency assumptions, allowing conditional interpretation of threshold directions. Across seven analytic-label benchmarks associated with ODE models, including a 15-compartment five-group SIR system, five-fold binary AUC was 0.999--1.000 and ordered-bracket accuracy was 0.951--0.998. REEBLRA complements rather than replaces mechanistic derivations, bridging simulation, machine learning, and reproduction-number analysis. An accompanying Shiny app supports implementation.
item.dc:creator: Jomar F. Rabajante, Norvin P. Bansilan, Maria Czarina T. Lagura-Arreza, Destiny SM. Lutero, Emerson R. Rico

item.title: Drivers of periodicity in population dynamic models of long-lived, large mammals
item.description: arXiv:2508.09037v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Population cycles are important components of many natural systems. Most studied in short-lived and small-bodied species, cycles frequently appear to be driven by density-dependent feedbacks. However, compelling evidence of cycles -- often more qualitative than quantitative -- also exists in large mammals. Among ungulates, both density-dependent vital rates and 'cohort effects' (lasting impacts of birth conditions on fecundity and survival) exist, but the implications of such feedbacks for oscillatory population dynamics have not been explored. Here, we present a synthetic model of ungulate population dynamics, parameterized for barren-ground caribou (Rangifer tarandus groenlandicus) and motivated by extensive Indigenous knowledge suggesting decades-long fluctuations in abundance. Caribou herds are theorized to be subject to both cohort effects and density dependence, and we linked these endogenous factors with environmental stochasticity to understand cycling. Using wavelet analysis, we characterized periodic phenomena and performed sensitivity analyses to clarify the drivers and characteristics of population cycles. We found that cohort effects, predominantly those impacting survival, can produce long-period oscillatory behavior across a wide range of environments and demographic structures. Our modeling framework is generalizable to other long-lived, large-bodied species with complex demography, and collectively, these efforts broaden the scope of inquiry into proximal drivers of population cycling.
item.dc:creator: Marron McConnell, William F. Fagan

item.title: Computing the final epidemic size distributions of a multi-type Galton--Watson process
item.description: arXiv:2606.03007v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide a theoretical ground to directly compute the final size distribution of a Galton--Watson process (GWP) from the implicit fixed point equations for its probability generating function (PGF). Firstly we show that valid identification of the final size PGF is ensured on any contour inside the unit polydisc. Furthermore, we derive error bounds for the PGF values on the contour, and establish the relationship between the differentiability of the offspring PGF and the final size PGF as a function of parameters that control the offspring distribution. Finally, we provide demonstrations using simulated and real-world data, and discuss potential identifiability issues regarding statistical inference that is associated with likelihoods that are not conditioned on extinction.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Okada, Hiroshi Nishiura
